# Epistle of Barnabas — Chapter 3 (SOPHIA Consensus)

**Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, Epistle of Barnabas 3
**Agent:** SOPHIA (Consensus)
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Consensus Translation

1. For again he says to them concerning these things: "Why do you fast to me? says the Lord. Is it so that your voice may be heard today with loud crying? This is not the fast I have chosen, says the Lord — that a man should merely humble himself.
2. Not even if you bow your neck like a ring and put on sackcloth and heap ashes under you — not even then shall you call it an acceptable fast."
3. But to us he says: "This is the fast I have chosen, says the Lord: Loose every bond of unrighteousness, untie the cords of violent oppression, release the broken and let them go free, and tear in pieces every unjust agreement.
4. Break your bread with the hungry; and if you see a naked person, clothe them; bring the homeless into your house; and if you see a person of lowly estate, do not despise them — neither you nor any of your household.
5. Then your light shall break forth early, and your healing shall arise quickly, and your righteousness shall go before you, and the glory of God shall encompass you.
6. Then shall you call, and God will hear you; and while you are still speaking he will say: 'Here I am.'"
7. So great a benefit it is, brothers, that the Lord has shown us these things and declared what kind of fast he has chosen. The service of the Lord is sweet and glorious, and it brings all things to us.

---

## Council Notes

- vv.1-6: Extended quotation from Isaiah 58:4-9 (LXX). The author uses this to argue that God's prophets redefined fasting as social justice — and that this is the tradition that belongs to Christians ("to us"), not to those who maintained physical fasting ("to them").
- v.7: "The service of the Lord is sweet and glorious" — *latreía* here is the whole system of true worship, contrasted with the rejected sacrificial latreía of chapter 2. The author sets up a complete replacement theology: right worship = social justice + inner transformation.
- The "to them / to us" distinction (vv.1-3) is Barnabas's consistent hermeneutical move: the prophets were actually addressing Christians, not the literal Jewish community.
